A.1:
Let me give you this whole business in three letters. A, S, A. Attitude, Schedule, Activity. I'll tell you what each one means, then show you why it works no matter how you start.

Attitude comes first, because everything flows from it. It's how you choose to show up: grateful, optimistic, coachable, with a servant's heart, and positive. We'll go deeper on it in the next lesson.

Schedule is second. We're one hundred percent virtual. Nobody is going to drive you to an office. So your calendar is your office. You being engaged and showing up is the office. And it has to be tight: when you start, when you dial, when you train, when you stop.

Activity is third. Dials, conversations, presentations, applications. Your Activity Planner tells you exactly how much you need for your goal, and the scoreboard never lies.

Here's why it works. I've watched very different starts. One agent didn't make a sale for thirty-seven days. Seven days a week, long days, nothing. He kept showing up, and today he leads one of the biggest teams in our company. Another agent took off in his very first month doing $50,000 right out of the gate. Another was a steady producer who grew into a great builder. Completely different results. But every one of them had the same three things: the right attitude, the right schedule, and the right activity.

That's why I can promise you this: if you do ASA in a big way, you will win. I just can't tell you when. It could be your first week. It could be a few days or weeks in. The only way you lose is if you stop before your day comes.

So, three letters: Attitude, Schedule, Activity. Do all three in a big way, and let the results catch up to you.
A.3:
There are two ways new agents start, and both are extremes. I'll show you both, then show you where to live.

Extreme one: the Hot Mess Express. They know almost nothing. They've got a writing number, they jump in the dial room, come off mute, and start reading a script they barely know. They sound rough. They fumble the application. But the person on the phone actually needs coverage, so sometimes that client works with them anyway. The Hot Mess Express probably gets somebody protected this week, and they're learning fast, because one hour of practical is worth forty hours of conceptual.

Extreme two: Perfect Prep. They take three months. Bookmarks organized, every carrier memorized, and the script rehearsed a hundred times. Then they get on the phone and still trip over the first objection, because no amount of preparation prepares you for your first real dial. And they've gone three months without earning a dollar, which is exactly when a lot of people quit.

Where you want to live is the middle. Be prepared: know the open and your opening objections cold. And be okay stumbling. You will stumble. That's not failure. That's the price of admission.

Two things make it easier. First, put your ego in the back seat. Anyone who would judge you has never done this, and everyone in our dial room has been exactly where you are. Second, remember what we actually do. We're not doing heart surgery. We're helping Miss Betty get a policy that pays her family when she's gone. If you fumble a little, Miss Betty will be okay. If you never call her, she won't.

So: not a hot mess, not perfect. Prepared enough, humble enough, and on the phone as soon as humanly possible.
S.1:
Let me walk you through our Winning Day in three blocks: the morning, the middle, and the night.

The morning. Our virtual office opens at 8:00 Eastern. The lights are on, so to speak, Zoom is on, and the dial room stays open all day, because that's our office. At 8:30 Eastern, Monday through Saturday, we do our Morning Kickoff together. We read from The Greatest Salesman in the World, we write our top ten goals, Brian Tracy style, and we do a little coaching on whatever came up yesterday. At 9:00 we're on the phones. That's 8:00 Central, and our veterans are up early. Your goal for the first block: get a sale before lunch. It takes the pressure off the whole rest of the day.

The middle. Around noon most weekdays there's a live training: the Builder's Call on Monday, the Winning System on Tuesday for your first week or two, SRS on Thursday, Shawn on Friday. Be there live. Then at 2:00, Monday through Friday, it's Nuts and Bolts. Bring the objection you couldn't handle and the application that confused you this morning, and we'll fix it together. Then back on the phones through the afternoon.

The night. Keep dialing into the evening, because a lot of people are home after five. Before you shut down, take five minutes to recap: what worked, and where you got stuck. Then log your numbers and your points on your Goal Card, lock down today's sales, and set tomorrow's number one target.

Two rules hold the whole day together. The thirty-second rule: anything that isn't a dial or a client and takes longer than thirty seconds waits until the end of the day. Got a question two hours into a dial block? Write it down, keep dialing, and bring it to Nuts and Bolts. And protect your prime dial hours. Errands, personal calls, even recruiting conversations go early, at lunch, or after work.

So: Kickoff and dials in the morning, training and Nuts and Bolts in the middle, dials and tracking at night. Block it in your calendar tonight.
S.2:
Now let's zoom out to the week. Three things: what my week actually looks like, the calls that anchor yours, and why the hours are what they are.

My week. I work six days. Sunday is church and family, every week. Monday through Wednesday, and usually Thursday, are long days, around twelve hours. Friday I'm usually done by five, because it's date night. Saturday I'm done by three or four, and some Saturdays that means Disney with the kids, a fringe benefit of living in Orlando. When my kid has a concert on Thursday, it goes on the calendar just like a dial block. If your brain jumps from thing to thing like mine, planning the breaks is what makes the work blocks actually happen. And before you start, if you have a family relying on you, sit down with them and write a wants-and-needs list. If it's just you, do it anyway, for your own situation. On the left, everything you and the people you're responsible for want and need. On the right, what you're willing to give up for a season to get it. Then walk them through your Winning Week, so three weeks in, nobody is surprised by your schedule.

The calls that anchor your week. Morning Kickoff at 8:30 Eastern, Monday through Saturday. Monday at noon, the Builder's Call, and Monday evening, our agency sales call. Tuesday at noon, the Winning System call. You'll only need it once or twice, to understand our leads and how we manage them. Thursday at noon, the SRS call, which is all about IULs and annuities. Friday at noon, Shawn's coaching call. That's probably the most important call of the week. And when you're new, Saturday is New Agent Orientation, where they walk through exactly how you get paid and what to focus on as a new agent.

Why the long hours? Some people compare this business to a forty-hour job. Compare it to owning a business instead, because that's what it actually is. A lot of franchise operators work sixty or seventy hours a week, and they don't even own the building. In the beginning we work big hours because we're new, we're learning, and we're going to fall on our faces a few times. As you get good, you earn your time back.

Your homework: block your Winning Week in your calendar, with the calls, the dial blocks, and your family time. Screenshot it and send it to your manager or mentor.

So: six days, family protected, the calls locked in, and big hours while you're new. That's the Winning Week.
AC.1:
Big goals get simple when you break them down. Three steps: your number, your production, and your day.

Your number. Open Agent Tools in the portal and build your Agent Success Plan. Let's use a real example. An agent I coached this week wants fifteen thousand a month take-home. That's a big goal, and it's a good one, because it's theirs.

Your production. Your plan turns that take-home number into what you need to sell. For fifteen thousand, it came out around thirty-three thousand a month in production. That's because what you deposit is the advance, minus your lead spend and your commission percentage. In reality, you'll make even more once all the months are paid, if your persistency is high. If the average policy is about fifteen hundred a year, that's about twenty-two sales a month. At twelve hundred, about twenty-seven. Over a six-day week, that's roughly six a week. About one sale a day. This isn't quantum physics. It's one family a day.

Your day. Now we push this over to the Optimum Activity Planner. It uses your real ratios: how many dials it takes to reach someone, how many of those let you present, and how many presentations buy. The planner turns your one sale a day into a daily dial number. Then you track your day on your Goal Card, and the next lesson shows you how. Whatever your planner says, three hundred fifty dials a day is our absolute floor.

Your turn-in: bring three things to your strategy call. Your take-home number, a screenshot of your Activity Planner, and your why. Don't just come to that meeting with "I want to make more money." Know the real why: why you're doing this, and who it's really for.

So: pick your number, let your plan turn it into sales, and let the planner turn it into dials.
AC.3:
What gets measured gets managed. You can't manage your effort if you're not measuring what goes into it. So let me show you the one tool that does that: your Goal Card. Three things: how points work, why forty is the number, and why points are the only thing you need to think about when you're new.

* [ON SCREEN: the Goal Card, daily view ]*

How points work. You log your activity in two-hour blocks across the day. You track your dials, because dials are your base input, but dials don't earn points. Points come from the things that actually matter. A contact, when you reach a real person, is one point. Set an appointment, two points. Give a presentation, three points. Make a sale, five points. So say you reach someone, that's one. You present to them, that's three more, so four. They buy, that's five more, so nine points from one person. And if you'd set an appointment with them earlier in the day, that's two more. One person can be worth up to eleven points.

Why forty. Forty points a day is very, very doable, and there are a lot of ways to get there. Say you reach twenty-two people, present to four of them, set one appointment, and close one. That's forty-one. A day with a ton of contacts, a few presentations and a few appointments gets you there too. Here's what we know: if you hit forty points a day, you will be wildly successful in this business. And the card does the math for you. Save it every night and you can compare today to yesterday, this week to last week, this month to last month. Put in your premium written and your hours, and it shows you what every dial and every hour is actually worth, and what it takes you to get one sale. That's your track record.

* [ON SCREEN: "What today's numbers say" panel ]*

Why points are all you think about. If you had a boss paying you by the hour and he said, "Track this every day," you'd do it, no matter what. Here, you're the boss. So be your own manager. Because if you're not tracking, nobody can coach you. Everybody thinks they made a million calls when they made seven. Everybody thinks they got fifty points, and when they finally track it, it was nine. So separate yourself from the result. Don't sit there thinking about sales and money. Just get your forty points, and the sales take care of themselves. It's like the gym. If you show up five days a week, even if all you do is walk the track, you'll start seeing what other people do, picking up new exercises, and getting results. It all starts with showing up and doing the basics. Your points are the basics. They're the last A in ASA: Activity. This is how we track it, and this is how we keep it strong.

So: points come from contacts, appointments, presentations and sales. Forty a day is the target. And you track them every single day, because what gets measured gets managed.
T.1:
Two tools run your call. I'll show you three things: the Script Navigator, the Product Wizard, and how they work together on a live call.

* [ON SCREEN: Script Navigator, Veteran script open ]*

The Script Navigator is your script and your client file in one. Pick the Veteran script, and it walks you through the call section by section. You don't have to read every word. As you type, it builds the client's profile for you. And it asks the follow-up questions you'd never know to ask. Type metformin, and it pops up: do they have diabetes, and what's their A1C? That's exactly what the underwriting system will want to know, so now you've already asked it.

* [ON SCREEN: click through to the Product Wizard ]*

When you have their health and budget, push one button and everything flows into the Product Wizard. The Wizard tells you which carriers are likely to approve this person, ranked by best fit for the client. Turn off any carriers you aren't contracted with yet, so it never recommends one you can't write.

* [ON SCREEN: carrier portal, then back to the Navigator ]*

Click through to the top carrier, run the quote in their portal, and put the numbers back into the Navigator. It shows you how to present three options: Maximum Coverage, Recommended, and Basic. When the client picks, every detail you need for the application is right there to copy and paste from the digital client profile you've built.

And your fallback never changes. If the tools confuse you mid-call, say: "I'm going to place you on a very brief soft hold while I speak to one of our senior underwriters to make sure we get you the best coverage for the best price. I'll be right back." Mute, ask the dial room, and we'll help you.

So: the Navigator runs the call, the Wizard picks the carrier, and the dial room always has your back. Bookmark both tools now.
0.0:
Welcome to Optimum Academy. I'm Jesse, and before you click anything else, I want to tell you three things: how this Academy is laid out, the one thing you should not do, and what I'm asking from you.

First, how this is laid out. There are two parts. Part one is Clear to Dial. It's twenty-one short lessons, and it's what you need before your first live call: the ASA foundation, your Winning Day and Winning Week, your numbers, your tools, the open, and your opening objections. Part two is Learn While Dialing. That's the full library: the whole call section by section, objections in depth, how you get paid, compliance, recruiting. You work through it in your first thirty days, between dial blocks, while you're actually on the phones. And it all starts with our model of success, three letters, ASA. That's your very next lesson.

Second, the one thing not to do. Do not wait to finish this whole Academy before you dial. One hour on the phone is worth forty hours of watching videos. Finish Clear to Dial, get in the live dial room, and keep learning while you work.

Third, what I'm asking from you. Contracting runs in parallel, so if you haven't submitted yours, do it today. And one question before we start: do I have your permission to hold you to your highest standards? Good. Because that's my job.

So: Clear to Dial gets you on the phones, the library makes you great while you work, and ASA is where it starts. Let's go.
1.3:
Your first dial should feel smooth, not like you're building the plane while flying it. Three things to set up before day one: your call tools, your carriers, and your follow-up stack.

Your call tools. Bookmark the Script Navigator and the Product Wizard. The Navigator runs your call and builds the client profile as you go. The Wizard tells you which carrier is likely to approve them. You'll learn both in the next lesson.

Your carriers. As your contracts come back, bookmark every carrier's agent portal and log in once, so you know your password works. When you're mid-call and the Wizard says Americo, you want to be one click away, not resetting a password while Miss Betty waits on hold.

Your follow-up stack. This is what turns a sale into a policy that stays on the books. Set up your Legacy Safeguard account; it's a real gift you give every client. Know where the client follow-up sequence is in the Agent Portal, under Resources, so you know what to say and when to say it. It's all copy and paste for you. And have thank-you cards ready to send every client right away. It's old school, but it's so worth it to keep your persistency high.

What about a CRM and a dialer? Not yet. You'll start by dialing your leads by hand. Once you're consistently hitting your dial number and want to go faster, that's when you add Goat CRM. Do the hard thing first, then make it easier.

Cheap and ready beats fancy and later. Work through the checklist attached to this lesson and you'll walk into day one like you've done it before.

So: tools bookmarked, carriers one-click away, follow-up ready. Then get on the phone.
4.3:
This is the Winning System. It's how you feed the number your Activity Planner gave you without betting the farm. Three things: where you start, how you grow, and the two numbers that tell you it's working.

Where you start. Leads are our raw material, and there are a lot of kinds: aged leads, fresh real-time leads, direct mail, telemarketed, Facebook and internet leads, referrals, and your own warm market. You start on aged leads, the inexpensive ones, about a dollar each. Why? Because when you're new, you're going to make mistakes, and it's a lot cheaper to learn on a dollar lead than on a fresh one. You manage every lead in GoatLeads.

How you grow. Month one, about five hundred dollars a week on aged leads, with a goal of about ten thousand in production. Month two, keep your five hundred on aged and add five hundred a week in fresh leads, with a goal of about twenty thousand. Month three, five hundred aged and a thousand fresh, with a goal of about thirty thousand. You're not reaching into your pocket for that growth. You're reinvesting what the leads already paid you. That's the parlay. And fresh leads are perishable. Work them within twenty-four hours, and triple-dial them across that first day. A fresh lead you sit on is money you threw away.

The two numbers. Only two numbers tell you if this is working. One: your cost per acquisition, what you spent on leads divided by the sales you made. Two: what you keep, not what you sold, but what's left after your leads. If those two numbers are healthy, keep reinvesting and scale up. If they're not, bring them to us and we'll find the fix with you.

This is taught live every Tuesday at noon Eastern. Come once or twice with your Activity Planner screenshot and your numbers, and we'll work them with you.

So: start on aged leads, parlay into fresh as you earn, and watch your cost per acquisition and what you keep.
2.6.1:
You've got their why, their budget, and their health. Now you educate and get the price. Three moves: the contrast, the benefits, and the price.

The contrast. Education isn't a lecture. It's a side-by-side, so the right answer is obvious. Say it plainly: "There are three types. Accidental only is cheap, but it only pays if you die in an accident. Term lasts ten to thirty years and then it expires. It's also usually only available to someone who's really healthy, and usually younger. Whole life is permanent. It never expires, it builds value, and the rate is locked for life." For a healthy client, mention a fourth option: more affordable permanent coverage. That's your bridge to IUL down the road. And if they already have a policy, never tell them it's bad. Say this: "That was a good option when you got it. Insurance is a lot like phones. The one you had worked; they just keep getting better. Let's see what's best for you today." You're comparing, not criticizing.

The benefits. Have them write these down: permanent, locked-in rate, living benefits, tax-free, and cash value. When they write it, they own it.

The price. On the call, your tools do the work. The Script Navigator already has their profile, so push it to the Product Wizard. The Wizard ranks the carriers likely to approve them. Go to that carrier, run the quote, and bring the numbers back into the Navigator to present. And if you're new, or anything feels confusing, use the soft hold, word for word: "I'm going to place you on a very brief soft hold while I speak to one of our senior underwriters to make sure we get you the best coverage for the best price. I'll be right back." Mute, ask the dial room, and we'll help you land it. That isn't weakness. It tells the client you care enough to get it right.

So: contrast the three types, have them write down the benefits, and get the price through your tools or through the room.
3.1:
The fastest way to get good is to learn next to people who are already winning. Our live dial room runs all day, every day, and it's your on-the-job training classroom. Three things: why you're in the room, the five rungs of the ladder, and how you earn solo.

Why you're in the room. You'll hear the open, the why, and the objections dozens of times before you ever say them. And when you're live with a client, the room is your backup. You'll also hear our best closers get told no, over and over. That's the job; nobody closes everyone. And that's why the script assumes you're off mute when you're on a call: you ask, and we help. When you're new, always come off mute. I can't help you if I can't hear you. It may be uncomfortable. Do it anyway, because it's the only way I can coach you. You can join the live dials starting today, even before your first call.

The ladder. Rung one: listen. Be in the room with the Script Navigator open and follow along. Rung two: shadow and take notes. Keep a tally of the objections you hear and how the closers handle them, and bring your list to Nuts and Bolts at two o'clock. Rung three: practice what you will say when another agent gets an objection; it's almost like you are answering the objection in real-time for them. Rung four: supervised calls. Dial your first aged leads with someone in the room listening, and soft-hold to the room on every quote. Record one or two of your calls and send them to your manager or mentor. We listen to where you started, where you got off track, and what you said when they told you no. Most of the time you'll hear the fix yourself. Rung five: solo.

Earning solo. The gate isn't a date on the calendar. It's a behavior. When you can run the whole script start to finish and handle the core objections without help, you're released and off to the races. Until then, you're always dialing in the dial room, off mute. Some people get there in a few days. Some take a few weeks. Both are fine.

So: live in the room, climb the ladder one rung at a time, and earn solo by what you can do, not by how long you've been here.
A.2:
People ask me why the A in ASA stands for attitude and not mindset. I'll give you three things: the difference between them, what our attitude looks like, and the quiet voice you need to watch for.

One, the difference. Mindset is what shows up. It's the thought that pops into your head when you wake up, when a client hangs up on you, when you check your bank account. You don't always choose it. Attitude is what you do with it. You can't always control the first thought. You can always control the next move. That's attitude, and that's why it's the A we train.

Two, what our attitude looks like. Gratitude first. Every morning at our 8:30 Kickoff we read, we write our goals, and we start grateful, because a grateful person is hard to discourage. Then optimism: the next call could be the one. And a servant's heart. We're helping families, not chasing checks. We're a Christian organization. We accept everybody, and we know who's in charge, which takes a lot of weight off your shoulders.

Three, the quiet voice. It won't tell you to quit. It's smarter than that. It says, "Sure, you'll make your calls today. But can you do this every single day for a year? No? Then why does today matter?" It makes the whole mountain feel so big that this one step feels pointless. Don't argue with that voice. Just make the next dial. The only step that matters is the one in front of you.

And attitude is contagious both ways. When yours slips, everyone feels it. When yours is strong, you lift the whole room.

So: mindset shows up, attitude is your choice. Start grateful. And when the quiet voice talks, answer it with a dial.
A.4:
Here's a lesson that took me years to learn. I'll give it to you in three parts: the same event, the mirror, and the word "next."

The same event. Say a policy falls off. If it's your very first policy, it feels like the end of the world. But let's say you'd sold ten policies and one fell off. You still had a great month, and you'd call it a numbers game. Same event both times. The only difference is the story you told yourself about it. That example is the entire insurance business. It's not good, it's not bad. It just is. My mentor and I used to joke about it: "Well, that's lesson number seven hundred twenty-eight." There's always another lesson, and you only have to pay for each one once.

The mirror. When someone else has a great day on the same kind of leads you had a rough day on, you have two choices. You can say, "They must have gotten lucky." Or you can look in the mirror and ask, "What did they do differently, and what can I do better?" Not to beat yourself up. To get better. Pick the mirror every time. And watch out for comparison. Comparison is the thief of all joy. If you downplay yourself, or make an excuse for someone else's success, it becomes easier to make excuses for yourself. We all have the same leads. Same talent, different skill. No one was born saying, "I want to be an insurance agent." The winners just worked really hard.

And the word "next." When someone hangs up on you, ask yourself honestly: was that going to be your client anyway? Was that someone you'd enjoy calling for policy reviews? Some will, some won't, so what? Next. Say it out loud if you need to. And know that leads come in runs. A quiet morning isn't a bad batch, and it isn't you. When I see you at seven tonight, I shouldn't be able to tell whether you made four sales or none.

Fall in love with the process, and let go of the result of any single call. When something goes wrong, don't freak out. It's part of the process.

So: same event, different story. Choose the mirror. And say "next."
A.5:
I want to prepare you for the hard part before it gets here, because the people who know the dip is coming are the ones who make it through. Three things: a story about someone else, a story about me, and a question for you.

A young agent on another team in our company went thirty-seven days without a single sale. Seven days a week, long days. Maybe he was nervous, maybe he wasn't dialing as much as he thought, maybe his attitude sucked, maybe he just sounded horrible on the phones, maybe he thought he was doing everything right even though all evidence showed he needed to make a shift. Nothing worked. But he knew it was him, because he was surrounded by people who were winning. Or better said, he surrounded himself with people who were winning. Then he made one sale. Then another. Today he leads one of the biggest organizations in the company. Literally, he's under 25 and a millionaire.

Now me. When I left a twenty-year corporate career to do this, I'd been a top salesperson and a sales executive. My first five months here, I made about twenty thousand dollars. Total. We had just moved to Florida, and my wife kept saying one thing: "I believe in you." I honestly didn't know if I could do it. But I was the first one in the Zoom room at 7:30 and the last one out at night, six and seven days a week. I was scared, some days I was barely dialing, and everyone around me was winning. What I did know was this: life insurance has been around for two hundred years, millions of families don't have enough, and the leads never run out. So the problem was me, and I could fix me. I refused to quit, and eventually it clicked.

So here's the question. If your first thirty-seven days look like his, will you still be here on day thirty-eight? Decide that now, while it's easy. Make sure you are willing to do the work and put in the effort this is going to take. Then when the hard week comes, you won't be deciding. You'll have already decided.

And here's why the dip happens. What you do today doesn't show up today. It shows up weeks from now. Time either promotes you or exposes you. So on the slow days, you're not failing. You're planting.

So: the dip is normal, it ends for the people who stay, and the decision to stay is made today.
A.6:
Stan Smith, one of the fastest-growing agency owners in our company, taught something on one of our Monday night calls that I want every new agent to have. Three steps: preach it, act it, become it.

Preach it. Pick who you're going to be and say it out loud. Every morning, every night, to your manager or mentor, in your journal, in the team chat. Say it to yourself most of all. When we write our goals at Morning Kickoff every day, that's preaching. Once you say it out loud, you've created accountability everywhere.

Act it. Because you're saying it, you start showing up like it's already true. If you said you're the one who's first in the dial room dialing, then you have to be in the dial room, dialing. Step one might be as small as showing up fifteen minutes earlier than you did yesterday and quickly calling your first lead.

Become it. Preach it long enough and act it long enough, and one day it isn't effort anymore. It's just who you are. "I'm just the one who's in the room before Kickoff getting some dials in. I'm just the one with the great attitude."

Two warnings. First, slumps start when you stop preaching. If you aren't saying anything, there's nothing to show up for and nobody to hold you to it. Second, if you're changing an old habit, give the new one twice as long as you spent on the old one. People know you for who you were until you've proven who you are long enough.

So here's your turn-in. Write one sentence that starts with "I'm the one who," and post it in our team chat today. Preach it. Then go act it.
AC.2:
Here's a tool I use on myself, and it stings a little. Three parts: the math, the hard thing first, and the omelet.

The math. At the end of the day, take your dials and divide them by the hours you worked. Say you worked ten hours and made a hundred dials. That's ten dials an hour. A dial where nobody picks up takes five or six seconds. Even if every dial took a full minute, that's ten minutes of real work in each hour. So what happened to the other fifty? Most of us believe we worked all day. The math tells the truth. The people who do well in this business aren't more talented. They're working the whole time they're working.

The hard thing first. New agents want to make the hard thing easier before they've ever done it. They want the CRM and the power dialer on day one. Don't. Dial by hand first and get used to the hard thing. When you're consistently hitting your number and your hands can't dial fast enough, that's when you add GOAT CRM with auto-dialing. Tools make a working process faster. They don't create one.

The omelet. Have you ever seen a chef flip an omelet? They make it look easy. Flipping an omelet feels weird the first time, and sometimes it ends up on the floor. Every chef has dropped a pile of them. The script is the same. It feels weird because you've never done it, not because it doesn't work. Run it twenty-seven more times, then tell me it doesn't work.

Tonight, divide your dials by your hours. Understand your actual working time, and hit your 40 points on the Goal Card tomorrow.

So: let the math tell you the truth, do the hard thing before you make it easy, and keep flipping the omelet.
